title: OOO Hack
author: Ethan Evans and Jason P. Yoong
summary: Ethan Evans and Jason Yoong describe a small visibility tactic: turning an Out Of Office message into a mini billboard that stands out to senior executives. Early in his career, Yoong included two or three interesting projects, recent work wins, and one or two insightful things he had learned, such as a TED Talk or article. The people who replied most were senior vice presidents and above, and one executive vice president asked for more talk recommendations, which led to regular hallway conversations that built rapport and his confidence presenting to her team. The authors advise writing separate messages for internal and external recipients, keeping personal messages casual, and keeping everything crisp enough to read on mobile. They add a recent personal example from a family vacation in Sydney, which drew a reply offering an introduction. The piece is short and ends with promotion of their courses.
points: An Out Of Office message can work as a mini billboard that signals growth, results and curiosity to senior people who would otherwise never see them.
Include two or three projects, recent wins and one or two insightful things you learned, so the reader has something to reply to.
The most frequent repliers were senior vice presidents and above, and a shared interest in talks turned into a lasting rapport with an executive.
Write separate internal and external versions, keep personal ones casual, and keep every version concise enough for a phone screen.
A well-crafted message makes it easy to reconnect with people and can generate unexpected introductions.
quotes: Early in my (Jason) career, I used my Out Of Office (OOO) message to stand out to senior executives.
Two to three interesting projects I was working on (e.g. co-chairing a non profit industry event, launched XYZ marketing campaign). Signaled my growth.
Recent work wins (e.g. press article, industry award). Signaled my results and credibility.
One to two insightful things I learned (e.g. TED Talk, article). This gave a peak into my curiosities to spark conversation.

Every time we met (e.g. hallway, meeting) we would briefly chat about the latest talk. This built rapport, trust, and made me more confident (and comfortable) presenting in front of her and her leadership team
For work emails, I created separate messages for internal recipients (usually including internal links to projects, wikis) and external partners.
